notes:
1. Indus Valley Civilization — Overview

  • The Indus Valley Civilization was one of the earliest urban civilizations of the world.
  • It is also called:
  • Harappan Civilization.
  • Indus Civilization.
  • The term Harappan Civilization is often preferred because many sites lie outside the Indus River valley.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indus Valley Civilization = Harappan Civilization

2. Chronology

The Harappan cultural sequence is broadly divided into:

  • Early Harappan Phase → c. 3300–2600 BCE.
  • Mature Harappan Phase → c. 2600–1900 BCE.
  • Late Harappan Phase → c. 1900–1300 BCE.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mature Harappan Urban Phase → c. 2600–1900 BCE

3. Bronze Age Civilization

  • The Harappan Civilization belonged to the Bronze Age.
  • Bronze is primarily an alloy of:
  • Copper.
  • Tin.
📌 Must-Memorise

Harappan Civilization → Bronze Age

4. Contemporary Civilizations

The Harappan Civilization was broadly contemporary with:

  • Mesopotamian Civilization.
  • Egyptian Civilization.

5. Geographical Extent

Harappan sites have been found across parts of present-day:

  • India.
  • Pakistan.
  • Afghanistan.

Its geographical extent was much larger than the Indus River valley alone.

6. Broad Boundaries

Important extreme sites traditionally used in examinations include:

  • North → Manda.
  • South → Daimabad.
  • East → Alamgirpur.
  • West → Sutkagendor.
📌 Must-Memorise

North → Manda

South → Daimabad

East → Alamgirpur

West → Sutkagendor

7. Manda

  • Manda is located in the Jammu region.
  • It represents the northern extent traditionally associated with Harappan distribution.

8. Daimabad

  • Daimabad is located in Maharashtra.
  • It is one of the southernmost sites associated with the wider Late Harappan cultural sphere.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Daimabad → Maharashtra

9. Alamgirpur

  • Alamgirpur is located in Uttar Pradesh.
  • It is regarded as the easternmost major Harappan site in conventional examinations.
📌 Must-Memorise

Alamgirpur → Uttar Pradesh → Eastern Extent

10. Sutkagendor

  • Sutkagendor was located near the Makran coast in present-day Pakistan.
  • It was strategically positioned near trade routes toward Iran and the Arabian Sea.

11. Name "Harappan Civilization"

  • The civilization is named after Harappa because Harappa was the first major site where the civilization was archaeologically identified.

12. Discovery of Harappa

  • Harappa was excavated by Daya Ram Sahni.
  • Excavation began in 1921.
📌 Must-Memorise

Harappa → Daya Ram Sahni → 1921

13. Discovery of Mohenjo-daro

  • Mohenjo-daro was excavated by R. D. Banerji.
  • Major excavation began in 1922.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mohenjo-daro → R. D. Banerji → 1922

14. John Marshall

  • Sir John Marshall was Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India.
  • He announced the discovery of the Indus Civilization to the wider world in 1924.
📌 Must-Memorise

John Marshall → Public Announcement → 1924

15. Harappa — Location

  • Harappa is located in present-day Punjab province of Pakistan.
  • It lies near the Ravi River.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Harappa → Ravi

16. Mohenjo-daro — Location

  • Mohenjo-daro is located in Sindh, Pakistan.
  • It lies near the Indus River.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mohenjo-daro → Indus

17. Meaning of Mohenjo-daro

  • Mohenjo-daro is commonly translated as "Mound of the Dead."
📌 TNPSC Favourite

Mohenjo-daro → Mound of the Dead

18. Major Harappan Sites

Important sites include:

  • Harappa.
  • Mohenjo-daro.
  • Dholavira.
  • Lothal.
  • Kalibangan.
  • Rakhigarhi.
  • Banawali.
  • Chanhudaro.
  • Surkotada.
  • Ropar.
  • Alamgirpur.
  • Sutkagendor.

19. Harappan Urban Character

The Mature Harappan Civilization was characterised by:

  • Planned cities.
  • Brick construction.
  • Drainage systems.
  • Standardised weights.
  • Craft specialisation.
  • Long-distance trade.

20. City Planning

Harappan cities frequently showed:

  • Grid-pattern streets.
  • Planned residential blocks.
  • Drainage channels.
  • Public structures.
  • Standardised brick sizes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Harappan Civilization → Highly Planned Urban Settlements

21. Grid Pattern

  • Streets commonly crossed one another at approximately right angles.
  • This created blocks of buildings.

22. Citadel

  • Many major Harappan settlements had an elevated or fortified sector conventionally called the citadel.
  • Important public structures were often located there.

23. Lower Town

  • The larger residential area is conventionally called the lower town.
  • Houses, workshops and streets occupied this zone.

24. Drainage System

  • Harappan cities are famous for sophisticated drainage.
  • Many houses were connected to street drains.
  • Drains were often covered.
📌 Must-Memorise

Harappan Urban Specialty → Drainage System

25. House Drains

  • Household wastewater commonly entered street drains.
  • Inspection openings and soak arrangements occurred at some sites.

26. Bathrooms

  • Many Harappan houses contained bathing areas with sloping floors and drains.

27. Wells

  • Numerous private and public wells have been found, especially at Mohenjo-daro.
  • This indicates organised urban water supply.

28. Building Materials

Harappans used:

  • Baked bricks.
  • Mud bricks.
  • Stone in regions where stone was readily available.

29. Standard Brick Ratio

A common Mature Harappan brick proportion was approximately:

1 : 2 : 4

for thickness : width : length.

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Harappan Brick Ratio → 1 : 2 : 4

30. Great Bath

  • The Great Bath was discovered at Mohenjo-daro.
  • It is one of the most famous Harappan structures.
📌 Must-Memorise

Great Bath → Mohenjo-daro

31. Great Bath Construction

Features included:

  • A large rectangular tank.
  • Brick construction.
  • Waterproofing.
  • Steps descending into the tank.
  • Surrounding rooms.

32. Function of Great Bath

  • Its exact function is unknown.
  • It is commonly interpreted as having had ritual or ceremonial significance.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Great Bath → Probable Ritual Use, Not Proven Swimming Pool

33. Granary — Harappa

  • Large brick structures conventionally interpreted as granaries were identified at Harappa.
  • Interpretations of some structures remain debated by archaeologists.

34. Great Granary — Mohenjo-daro

  • A major building at Mohenjo-daro was historically interpreted as a granary.
  • Modern archaeological interpretations are more cautious about its exact function.

35. Assembly Hall

  • Large pillared structures found at Mohenjo-daro have been interpreted as public or assembly buildings.

36. Lothal

  • Lothal is located in Gujarat.
  • It was excavated by S. R. Rao.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lothal → Gujarat → S. R. Rao

37. Lothal Dockyard

  • Lothal is famous for a large brick-lined basin traditionally identified as a dockyard.
  • It indicates the importance of maritime trade.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dockyard → Lothal

38. Lothal and Maritime Trade

Lothal had access to:

  • Gulf of Khambhat.
  • Arabian Sea trade networks.

39. Lothal Bead Industry

  • Lothal was an important centre of bead manufacture.
  • Carnelian beads were among its well-known craft products.

40. Lothal Rice Evidence

  • Archaeological evidence associated with rice has been reported from Lothal and some other Harappan-related contexts.
  • Wheat and barley remained more prominent staple crops across much of the civilization.

41. Dholavira

  • Dholavira is located on Khadir Bet in the Rann of Kachchh, Gujarat.
  • It is one of the largest and most distinctive Harappan cities in India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dholavira → Gujarat → Khadir Bet

42. Excavator of Dholavira

  • Dholavira was extensively excavated under R. S. Bisht.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dholavira → R. S. Bisht

43. Dholavira Urban Planning

Dholavira is notable for:

  • Sophisticated water management.
  • Large reservoirs.
  • Stone construction.
  • Distinct urban divisions.
  • Large inscription/signboard.

44. Dholavira Water Management

  • Rainwater and seasonal runoff were stored in large reservoirs.
  • Channels directed water into storage structures.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dholavira → Advanced Water Conservation

45. Dholavira Signboard

  • A large set of Harappan signs was discovered at Dholavira.
  • It is among the most striking examples of Harappan writing in a public architectural context.

46. Dholavira Stadium / Ceremonial Ground

  • Dholavira contains a large open area sometimes interpreted as a stadium or ceremonial ground.
  • Its precise use remains debated.

47. Kalibangan

  • Kalibangan is located in Rajasthan.
  • It lies on the Ghaggar River system.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kalibangan → Rajasthan → Ghaggar

48. Kalibangan Excavations

  • Kalibangan was excavated principally by B. B. Lal and B. K. Thapar.

49. Ploughed Field — Kalibangan

  • Archaeologists discovered evidence interpreted as a ploughed agricultural field at Kalibangan.
  • Cross-furrows suggest planned cultivation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ploughed Field → Kalibangan

50. Fire Altars — Kalibangan

  • Structures interpreted as fire altars were discovered at Kalibangan.
  • Similar ritual installations have been reported at some other Harappan sites.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kalibangan → Fire Altars

51. Earthquake Evidence — Kalibangan

  • Archaeological studies have suggested that an earlier settlement at Kalibangan may have been damaged by an earthquake before the Mature Harappan phase.

52. Rakhigarhi

  • Rakhigarhi is located in Haryana.
  • It is among the largest known Harappan urban settlements.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rakhigarhi → Haryana

53. Importance of Rakhigarhi

Archaeological remains include:

  • Residential structures.
  • Streets.
  • Drainage.
  • Burials.
  • Craft activity.

54. Banawali

  • Banawali is located in Haryana.
  • Both Early and Mature Harappan cultural remains have been found there.

55. Banawali Town Plan

  • Banawali shows planned settlement features but differs in layout from some classic grid-planned Harappan cities.

56. Chanhudaro

  • Chanhudaro is located in Sindh, Pakistan.
  • It was an important craft-production centre.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chanhudaro → Bead-Making / Craft Centre

57. Chanhudaro — Citadel Trap

  • Chanhudaro is often noted for lacking a clearly identified massive citadel comparable to some major Harappan centres.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite Trap

Chanhudaro → Important Harappan City Without Prominent Citadel

58. Surkotada

  • Surkotada is located in Gujarat.
  • It was a fortified Harappan settlement.

59. Horse Evidence — Surkotada

  • Animal remains from Surkotada have sometimes been identified as horse remains.
  • The identification has been debated among specialists.
📌 TNPSC Caution

Surkotada → Horse Evidence Often Asked, But Archaeological Identification Is Debated

60. Ropar / Rupnagar

  • Ropar is located in Punjab, India.
  • It lies near the Sutlej River.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ropar → Sutlej

61. Kot Diji

  • Kot Diji is in Sindh.
  • It is important for understanding the Early Harappan phase.

62. Amri

  • Amri is another important pre-/Early Harappan site in Sindh.

63. Mehrgarh

  • Mehrgarh is much earlier than the Mature Harappan Civilization.
  • It is located in Balochistan.
  • It provides important evidence for early farming and settled life in northwestern South Asia.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Mehrgarh → Neolithic/Early Farming Precursor

Not a Mature Harappan City

64. Agriculture

Major Harappan crops included:

  • Wheat.
  • Barley.
  • Pulses.
  • Sesame.
  • Mustard.

Cotton was also cultivated.

65. Cotton

  • The Harappans were among the earliest known cultivators and users of cotton.
  • Cotton textiles were known in the civilization.
📌 Must-Memorise

Harappans → Early Cotton Cultivation

66. Wheat

  • Wheat was an important food crop.
  • It was cultivated in fertile river plains and suitable regions.

67. Barley

  • Barley was another major cereal crop of the Harappans.

68. Irrigation

  • Agriculture depended significantly on seasonal river flooding and local water-management practices.
  • Evidence for large centrally built canal systems comparable to later civilizations is limited.

69. Animal Husbandry

Harappans domesticated animals such as:

  • Cattle.
  • Buffalo.
  • Sheep.
  • Goat.
  • Pig.

70. Humped Bull

  • The humped zebu bull appears frequently in Harappan representations.
  • Cattle were economically important.

71. Horse

  • Horse remains are rare and disputed in Mature Harappan contexts.
  • The horse was not a dominant feature of Harappan material culture.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Horse → Not a Characteristic Harappan Animal

72. Elephant

  • Elephants were known to the Harappans.
  • They appear on seals and in archaeological remains.

73. Rhinoceros

  • Rhinoceros appears in Harappan seal imagery.

74. Camel

  • Camel remains are known from Harappan contexts.

75. Trade

Harappans participated in:

  • Internal trade.
  • Regional trade.
  • Long-distance trade.
  • Maritime trade.

76. Mesopotamian Trade

  • Mesopotamian texts refer to a region called Meluhha.
  • Many historians identify Meluhha with the Harappan/Indus region.
📌 Must-Memorise

Meluhha → Harappan Region in Mesopotamian Records

77. Mesopotamia

Trade contacts connected the Harappan world with:

  • Mesopotamia.
  • Persian Gulf.
  • Oman region.
  • Iranian plateau.

78. Dilmun

  • Dilmun was an important Persian Gulf intermediary in ancient trade.
  • It is commonly associated with Bahrain and neighbouring Gulf regions.

79. Magan

  • Mesopotamian texts mention Magan.
  • It is generally associated with Oman and surrounding areas.
📌 TNPSC Memory

Meluhha → Indus

Dilmun → Bahrain

Magan → Oman

80. Export Commodities

Harappan exports probably included:

  • Beads.
  • Cotton textiles.
  • Shell products.
  • Timber.
  • Ivory.
  • Semi-precious stones.

81. Imported Materials

Harappans acquired materials such as:

  • Copper.
  • Tin.
  • Silver.
  • Gold.
  • Lapis lazuli.

from different regions.

82. Lapis Lazuli

  • Lapis lazuli was obtained mainly from Badakhshan in Afghanistan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lapis Lazuli → Badakhshan

83. Copper

  • Copper came from several sources.
  • Rajasthan's Khetri region was an important potential source.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Copper → Khetri, Rajasthan

84. Gold

  • Gold was obtained through trade from several regions, including parts of southern India according to conventional interpretations.

85. Shell

  • Shell objects were made from marine shells obtained from coastal regions.
  • Shell-working was a specialised craft.

86. Standardised Weights

  • Harappans used highly standardised stone weights.
  • This indicates organised trade and measurement systems.
📌 Must-Memorise

Harappans → Standardised Weights and Measures

87. Weight System

  • Harappan weights followed regular mathematical progression.
  • Binary-type sequences were important in smaller units.

88. Measures

  • Standardised measuring scales have also been found.
  • Lothal yielded an important measuring scale.

89. Craft Specialisation

Important Harappan crafts included:

  • Bead making.
  • Pottery.
  • Metalworking.
  • Shell working.
  • Seal carving.
  • Textile production.

90. Bead Making

Materials included:

  • Carnelian.
  • Agate.
  • Lapis lazuli.
  • Faience.
  • Shell.

91. Carnelian

  • Carnelian beads were important luxury goods.
  • Chanhudaro and Lothal were important bead-making centres.

92. Faience

  • Faience is a glazed non-clay material used for:
  • Beads.
  • Bangles.
  • Small objects.

93. Metallurgy

Harappans used:

  • Copper.
  • Bronze.
  • Gold.
  • Silver.
  • Lead.

94. Iron

  • Iron was not a characteristic metal of the Mature Harappan Civilization.
📌 Must-Memorise

Harappans → No Regular Iron Technology

95. Bronze Dancing Girl

  • A famous bronze figurine known as the Dancing Girl was discovered at Mohenjo-daro.
  • It was made by the lost-wax casting technique.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dancing Girl → Mohenjo-daro → Bronze → Lost-Wax

96. Lost-Wax Technique

  • A wax model is covered with clay.
  • Wax is melted out.
  • Molten metal is poured into the mould.

97. Priest-King

  • A famous steatite male figure popularly called the Priest-King was found at Mohenjo-daro.
  • The title is conventional; his actual identity is unknown.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Priest-King → Conventional Name, Identity Unknown

98. Red Sandstone Male Torso

  • A red sandstone male torso was discovered at Harappa.
  • It demonstrates sophisticated sculptural skill.

99. Terracotta Figurines

  • Numerous terracotta human and animal figurines have been found.
  • Some female figurines have traditionally been interpreted as fertility or mother-goddess figures, though their exact meaning is uncertain.

100. Pottery

Typical Harappan pottery was:

  • Wheel-made.
  • Often red.
  • Decorated with black painted designs.
📌 Must-Memorise

Harappan Pottery → Red Ware with Black Designs

101. Painted Motifs

Common motifs include:

  • Geometric patterns.
  • Plants.
  • Animals.

102. Seals

  • Thousands of seals have been discovered.
  • Most are made of steatite.
  • They commonly carry:
  • Animal figures.
  • Short inscriptions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Harappan Seals → Mostly Steatite

103. Unicorn Seal

  • The so-called unicorn is the most frequently represented animal motif on Harappan seals.
📌 TNPSC Favourite

Most Common Seal Motif → Unicorn

104. Pashupati Seal

  • A famous seal from Mohenjo-daro depicts a seated horned figure surrounded by animals.
  • John Marshall interpreted it as a possible proto-Shiva/Pashupati figure.
  • This interpretation remains debated.
📌 TNPSC Caution

Pashupati Interpretation → Proposed, Not Proven

105. Seal Functions

Seals may have been used for:

  • Identification.
  • Trade.
  • Ownership.
  • Administrative purposes.

Their exact functions may have varied.

106. Harappan Script

  • Harappans used a distinctive script.
  • It remains undeciphered.
📌 Must-Memorise

Harappan Script → Undeciphered

107. Nature of Script

  • Most inscriptions are short.
  • They appear on:
  • Seals.
  • Pottery.
  • Tablets.
  • Metal objects.
  • Other artefacts.

108. Direction of Writing

  • Many inscriptions appear to have been written from right to left.
  • Some examples show different arrangements.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Harappan Script → Commonly Right to Left

109. Number of Signs

  • Hundreds of distinct signs have been identified.
  • The exact number depends on how variants are classified.

110. Why Script Remains Undeciphered

Major difficulties include:

  • Short inscriptions.
  • No confirmed bilingual inscription.
  • Unknown underlying language.

111. Language of Harappans

  • The language represented by the script is unknown.
  • Dravidian and other linguistic hypotheses have been proposed, but no interpretation has been conclusively established.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Harappan Language → Not Definitively Known

112. Religion — Archaeological Evidence

Harappan religious beliefs are reconstructed mainly from:

  • Seals.
  • Figurines.
  • Burials.
  • Ritual structures.

No Harappan religious text has been deciphered.

113. Female Figurines

  • Some female terracotta figurines have been interpreted as fertility-related figures.
  • Their exact religious significance remains uncertain.

114. Sacred Trees

  • Trees such as pipal appear in Harappan imagery.
  • This suggests ritual or symbolic significance.

115. Animal Symbolism

Animals shown in Harappan art include:

  • Bull.
  • Elephant.
  • Rhinoceros.
  • Tiger.
  • Buffalo.
  • Unicorn motif.

116. Fire Ritual Evidence

  • Fire-altars or fire-related installations have been reported at:
  • Kalibangan.
  • Lothal and some other sites.

Interpretations vary by context.

117. Temple Evidence

  • No monumental temple comparable to Mesopotamian ziggurats or Egyptian temples has been securely identified in Harappan cities.
📌 Must-Memorise

Harappans → No Clearly Identified Monumental Temples

118. Palace Evidence

  • No unmistakable royal palace has been identified.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Harappan Cities → No Confirmed Palace

119. Political Organisation

  • The exact form of Harappan government is unknown.
  • Standardisation across a vast area indicates strong social and economic coordination.
  • Clear evidence for kings or a royal dynasty is absent.

120. Absence of Royal Monuments

Unlike Egypt and Mesopotamia, Harappan archaeology has not revealed:

  • Giant royal tombs.
  • Monumental statues of kings.
  • Clearly identified palaces.

121. Social Organisation

Evidence suggests:

  • Occupational specialisation.
  • Differences in house size.
  • Organised labour.
  • Extensive trade networks.

Exact social classes cannot be reconstructed with certainty.

122. Burial Practices

Harappans generally buried their dead.

Burials may contain:

  • Pottery.
  • Ornaments.
  • Personal objects.

123. Cemetery R-37

  • Cemetery R-37 at Harappa is an important Harappan burial ground.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cemetery R-37 → Harappa

124. Coffin Burial

  • Evidence interpreted as coffin burial has been found at Harappa.

125. Double Burial

  • Some sites have produced burials containing more than one individual.
  • Burial practices varied across the Harappan world.

126. Food

Harappan diet included:

  • Wheat.
  • Barley.
  • Pulses.
  • Sesame.
  • Dates.
  • Animal products.
  • Fish in suitable regions.

127. Fishing

  • Fish bones and fishing-related evidence indicate fishing was important in riverine and coastal settlements.

128. Clothing

  • Archaeological evidence suggests use of cotton.
  • Wool may also have been used.

129. Ornaments

Harappan men and women used ornaments made from:

  • Gold.
  • Silver.
  • Copper.
  • Shell.
  • Faience.
  • Semi-precious stones.

130. Bangles

  • Bangles made from shell, terracotta and other materials are common finds.

131. Toys

Terracotta toys include:

  • Carts.
  • Animals.
  • Figurines.
  • Whistles and other objects.

132. Bullock Cart

  • Terracotta models suggest use of wheeled carts.
  • Bullock carts probably played an important role in land transport.

133. Boats

  • Boats appear in Harappan representations.
  • Maritime trade and river transport were important.

134. Harappan Economy

The economy rested on:

  • Agriculture.
  • Animal husbandry.
  • Craft production.
  • Internal trade.
  • Long-distance trade.

135. Urban–Rural Relationship

  • Cities depended on surrounding rural settlements for:
  • Grain.
  • Animals.
  • Raw materials.
  • Rural settlements depended on towns for manufactured goods and exchange.

136. Standardisation

Harappan standardisation is visible in:

  • Bricks.
  • Weights.
  • Seals.
  • Craft techniques.
  • Urban planning.

137. Harappan Political Unity — Caution

  • Standardisation suggests broad cultural integration.
  • It does not by itself prove that the entire civilization was ruled by a single emperor.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Cultural Uniformity ≠ Proven Centralised Empire

138. Harappan Decline

The urban phase declined after approximately 1900 BCE.

Major cities were gradually:

  • Abandoned.
  • Reduced in size.
  • Reorganised.

139. Decline Was Gradual

  • The civilization did not disappear suddenly everywhere.
  • Urban centres declined while regional Late Harappan cultures continued.
📌 Must-Memorise

Harappan Decline → Gradual and Regional

140. Factors Suggested for Decline

Possible factors include:

  • Climatic change.
  • Weakening monsoon.
  • River-course changes.
  • Repeated flooding in some regions.
  • Decline in long-distance trade.
  • Ecological stress.
  • Population movement.

No single explanation accounts for every region.

141. Aryan Invasion Theory — Modern Caution

  • An older theory attributed Harappan collapse to a large-scale Aryan invasion.
  • Archaeological evidence does not support a simple invasion as the sole explanation for the civilization's decline.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Harappan Decline → Not Explained by a Single Proven Invasion

142. River Changes

  • Changes in river systems, including channels in the Ghaggar-Hakra region, affected settlement patterns.
  • River history in this region is complex and continues to be studied.

143. Climate Change

  • Increasing aridity and weakening monsoon conditions are considered important factors in the transformation of Harappan settlement patterns.

144. Flooding

  • Mohenjo-daro shows evidence of repeated rebuilding and flood-related deposits.
  • Floods may have contributed locally to urban problems.

145. Trade Decline

  • Changes in Mesopotamia and Persian Gulf trade networks may have weakened Harappan long-distance commerce.

146. De-Urbanisation

  • After the Mature Harappan phase, large cities declined.
  • Population shifted toward:
  • Smaller settlements.
  • Eastern regions.
  • Rural economies.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Post-1900 BCE → De-Urbanisation

147. Late Harappan Cultures

  • Harappan traditions continued after major urban centres declined.
  • Regional Late Harappan cultures developed in different areas.

148. Cemetery H Culture

  • Cemetery H at Harappa is associated with the Late Harappan phase.
  • It shows changes in pottery and burial customs.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cemetery H → Late Harappan

149. Harappan Legacy

Important continuities often discussed include:

  • Craft traditions.
  • Agricultural practices.
  • Settlement traditions.
  • Certain symbols and cultural practices.

Direct continuity for specific religious practices must be assessed cautiously.

150. India — Major Harappan Sites by State

Gujarat:

  • Dholavira.
  • Lothal.
  • Surkotada.

Haryana:

  • Rakhigarhi.
  • Banawali.

Rajasthan:

  • Kalibangan.

Punjab:

  • Ropar.

Uttar Pradesh:

  • Alamgirpur.

Maharashtra:

  • Daimabad.

151. Gujarat and Harappan Civilization

Gujarat was important for:

  • Coastal trade.
  • Craft production.
  • Marine resources.
  • Harappan urban expansion.

152. Haryana and Harappan Civilization

  • Haryana contains a very large concentration of Harappan settlements.
  • Rakhigarhi and Banawali are among the most important.

153. Rajasthan and Harappan Civilization

  • Kalibangan is the major Rajasthan site.
  • It provides key evidence for:
  • Early Harappan settlement.
  • Ploughed field.
  • Fire installations.

154. Punjab and Harappan Civilization

  • Ropar represents Harappan expansion along the Sutlej.
  • Harappa itself lies in present-day Pakistani Punjab.

155. Harappa — Key Facts

Harappa:

  • Punjab, Pakistan.
  • Ravi River.
  • Excavated by Daya Ram Sahni.
  • 1921.
  • Cemetery R-37.
  • Granary-type structures.

156. Mohenjo-daro — Key Facts

Mohenjo-daro:

  • Sindh, Pakistan.
  • Indus River.
  • R. D. Banerji.
  • 1922.
  • Great Bath.
  • Dancing Girl.
  • Priest-King.
  • Pashupati seal.

157. Lothal — Key Facts

Lothal:

  • Gujarat.
  • S. R. Rao.
  • Dockyard/basin.
  • Bead industry.
  • Maritime trade.
  • Measuring scale.

158. Dholavira — Key Facts

Dholavira:

  • Gujarat.
  • Khadir Bet.
  • R. S. Bisht.
  • Reservoirs.
  • Stone architecture.
  • Large signboard.
  • Distinct urban divisions.

159. Kalibangan — Key Facts

Kalibangan:

  • Rajasthan.
  • Ghaggar.
  • Ploughed field.
  • Fire-altars.
  • Early and Mature Harappan remains.

160. Rakhigarhi — Key Facts

Rakhigarhi:

  • Haryana.
  • One of the largest Harappan sites.
  • Urban settlement.
  • Burials.
  • Craft production.

161. Chanhudaro — Key Facts

Chanhudaro:

  • Sindh.
  • Craft centre.
  • Bead manufacturing.
  • Often noted for absence of a prominent citadel.

162. Surkotada — Key Facts

Surkotada:

  • Gujarat.
  • Fortified settlement.
  • Horse-remain claim, though debated.

163. Harappan Sites — River Pairings

  • Harappa → Ravi.
  • Mohenjo-daro → Indus.
  • Ropar → Sutlej.
  • Kalibangan → Ghaggar.
  • Lothal → Coastal/estuarine Gujarat setting.

164. Site–Discovery Pairings

  • Harappa → Daya Ram Sahni.
  • Mohenjo-daro → R. D. Banerji.
  • Lothal → S. R. Rao.
  • Dholavira → R. S. Bisht.

  • Dancing Girl → Mohenjo-daro.
  • Priest-King → Mohenjo-daro.

167. Material–Source Pairings

  • Lapis lazuli → Badakhshan.

168. Harappan Innovations — Exam View

High-yield features include:

  • Urban planning.
  • Drainage.
  • Standardised bricks.
  • Standardised weights.
  • Seal system.
  • Long-distance trade.
  • Water management.
  • Specialised crafts.

169. Harappan Features NOT Securely Found

No clear evidence for:

  • Iron technology.
  • Monumental royal palace.
  • Monumental temple.
  • Deciphered literature.
  • Identified king list.
📌 Must-Memorise

Harappan Script Undeciphered → No Historical King List

170. Harappan vs Vedic — Basic Exam Distinction

Harappan Civilization:

  • Urban.
  • Bronze Age.
  • Planned cities.
  • Script present but undeciphered.

Early Vedic society:

  • More pastoral-rural in its early phase.
  • Sanskrit/Vedic textual tradition.
  • Different archaeological-cultural context.

171. Harappan Writing vs Vedic Literature

  • Harappans left inscriptions but their script is undeciphered.
  • Vedic society is known extensively through preserved oral-textual traditions.

172. Harappan Urbanisation

The civilization represents India's earliest major phase of urbanisation.

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

First Urbanisation of Indian Subcontinent → Harappan Civilization

173. Second Urbanisation — Comparison

  • The rise of towns in the Ganga valley around the first millennium BCE is often described as India's Second Urbanisation.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

First Urbanisation → Harappan

Second Urbanisation → Ganga Valley / Mahajanapada Age

174. Environmental Diversity

Harappan settlements occupied:

  • River plains.
  • Semi-arid regions.
  • Coastal zones.
  • Islands.
  • Highland margins.

This explains regional variation in economy and architecture.

175. Water Management — Dholavira vs Mohenjo-daro

Dholavira:

  • Large reservoirs.
  • Rainwater/runoff harvesting.

Mohenjo-daro:

  • Numerous wells.
  • Urban drainage.
  • Great Bath.

176. Maritime Trade — Lothal

  • Lothal is the site most commonly linked with organised maritime commerce in TNPSC examinations.

177. Agriculture — Kalibangan

  • Kalibangan's ploughed field provides direct archaeological evidence of agricultural practice.

178. Craft Production — Chanhudaro

  • Chanhudaro is especially important for specialised manufacture rather than monumental public architecture.

179. Script — Major Exam Facts

  • Undeciphered.
  • Short inscriptions.
  • Mostly on seals and small objects.
  • Often right-to-left.
  • No confirmed bilingual text.

180. Economy — Major Exam Facts

  • Agriculture.
  • Animal husbandry.
  • Craft production.
  • Long-distance trade.
  • Standardised weights.

181. Society — Major Exam Facts

  • Urban differentiation existed.
  • Exact caste or class system cannot be reconstructed.
  • No deciphered textual evidence explains social hierarchy.

182. Religion — Major Exam Facts

Possible evidence includes:

  • Horned figure.
  • Female figurines.
  • Sacred trees.
  • Animal symbolism.
  • Fire installations.

But exact beliefs remain uncertain.

183. Harappan Decline — Major Exam Facts

Likely combination of:

  • Climate change.
  • River changes.
  • Trade disruption.
  • Flooding in certain areas.
  • Ecological stress.
  • De-urbanisation.
